phrase_variants: we never went to the moon

conceptual.claim_predicate: the Apollo moon landings did not occur as officially documented; the evidence presented to the public was fabricated

entities.instrument: film production, photography manipulation, and institutional control of information

conceptual.causal_structure: NASA and the U.S. government, through technical deception and media control, created false evidence of moon landings and presented it to the public as authentic historical fact

attestation_log.source_title: Moon landing conspiracy theories — Wikipedia (citing Chaikin 1994 and contemporaneous accounts)
attestation_log.lexical_form_seen: the moon landing was faked / moon landing conspiracy ideas
attestation_log.exact_quote: Doubts about the authenticity of the Apollo Moon landings first appeared in December 1968, when Apollo 8 was launched.
attestation_log.evidence: Multiple secondary historians (Chaikin 1994, Wikipedia synthesis) report that informal oral skepticism and fringe claims that the landing was staged circulated immediately after Apollo 8 (Dec 1968) and Apollo 11 (July 1969). No primary text with the exact diagnostic n-grams has been recovered from this period; this entry records the attested oral/informal origin window, not a specific document. Confidence is limited because no primary-source text with the diagnostic phrasing has been located for this period.
attestation_log.role_evidence: Represents the earliest attested window of the claim's existence per historians, but no recoverable primary document with the diagnostic n-grams survives from this moment.
attestation_log.cited_via: Wikipedia / multiple secondary historians citing Andrew Chaikin's 'A Man on the Moon' (1994) and other sources
attestation_log.verification_notes: no fuzzy chunk of quote found in page

attestation_log.source_title: "Did Man Land on the Moon?" — book by James J. Cranny
attestation_log.author: James J. Cranny
attestation_log.lexical_form_seen: Did man land on the Moon? [title implies faked landing]
attestation_log.exact_quote: The first book on the subject ("Did man land on the Moon?") was issued in 1970 by the Texas mathematician James J. Cranny.
attestation_log.evidence: Cited in Metapedia and Simple English Wikipedia as the first book on the subject, published 1970 in Texas. The title itself is a close lexical variant of the 'never went to the moon' framing. However, no digitized primary text has been located, and the exact internal phrasing of the book is unknown. Confidence is moderate due to secondhand citation only.
attestation_log.role_evidence: Described by multiple secondary sources as the first book-length articulation of the moon-landing-as-hoax claim, predating Kaysing's 1976 work.
attestation_log.cited_via: Metapedia Moon Hoax article (secondary); original book not digitally available
attestation_log.verification_notes: no fuzzy chunk of quote found in page

attestation_log.source_title: Moon-landing hoax still lives on. But why? — Space.com
attestation_log.exact_quote: The James Bond movie "Diamonds Are Forever," for example, had a joke about faked moon landings just two years later, in 1971.
attestation_log.evidence: Space.com (citing the 1971 film 'Diamonds Are Forever') documents that the phrase 'faked moon landings' was already culturally legible enough to be used as a joke in a mainstream Hollywood film just two years after Apollo 11. The film itself is the dated artifact; the Space.com article is the documenting source.
attestation_log.role_evidence: A mainstream Hollywood film referencing 'faked moon landings' as a recognizable joke indicates the framing had already entered popular culture by 1971.

attestation_log.source_title: We Never Went to the Moon: America's Thirty Billion Dollar Swindle
attestation_log.author: Bill Kaysing and Randy Reid
attestation_log.lexical_form_seen: We Never Went to the Moon
attestation_log.exact_quote: We Never Went to the Moon: America's Thirty Billion Dollar Swindle
attestation_log.evidence: Self-published June 3, 1976 (Eden Press, Fountain Valley CA; OCLC 19542836). The title itself is the canonical diagnostic n-gram 'never went to the moon.' Confirmed by Wikipedia, Amazon, eBay, Goodreads, and multiple scholarly secondary sources. This is the most widely cited originating text for the modern framing.
attestation_log.role_evidence: Universally credited by historians, journalists, and academics as the foundational text that launched the modern moon-landing-hoax framing into broad public circulation; directly inspired subsequent films, documentaries, and online communities.
attestation_log.verification_notes: no fuzzy chunk of quote found in page

attestation_log.source_title: Capricorn One (film) — documented via Rolling Stone and Manchester University
attestation_log.author: Peter Hyams (director)
attestation_log.lexical_form_seen: moon landing was staged / faked landing
attestation_log.exact_quote: The 1978 release of a film called Capricorn One...did much to promote the idea that the moon landing was staged.
attestation_log.evidence: The 1978 film Capricorn One depicted a faked government space mission and is documented by Rolling Stone, Manchester University, Space.com, and PolitiFact as a major amplifier of the 'moon landing was staged' framing. The film's plot directly mirrors the Kaysing thesis. Multiple sources confirm its 1978 release date.
attestation_log.role_evidence: Multiple independent sources credit Capricorn One with propelling the 'staged moon landing' framing into mainstream popular culture in the post-Watergate era.

attestation_log.source_title: "The Flat-out Truth: Earth Orbits? Moon Landings? A Fraud! Says This Prophet" — Science Digest
attestation_log.author: Robert J. Schadewald
attestation_log.exact_quote: Science Digest, "The Flat-out Truth: Earth Orbits? Moon Landings? A Fraud! Says This Prophet," July 1980
attestation_log.evidence: Cited in Wikipedia's Moon landing conspiracy theories article (with archive link) and PolitiFact's bibliography. Published July 1980 in Science Digest (Hearst Magazines). The title contains a close lexical variant of the diagnostic framing ('Moon Landings? A Fraud!'). The Flat Earth Society's formal accusation that NASA faked the landings is also dated to 1980 by multiple sources.
attestation_log.role_evidence: A national magazine article in 1980 brought the 'moon landings are a fraud' framing to a mainstream readership, amplifying Kaysing's earlier self-published work.
attestation_log.cited_via: PolitiFact (documenting source); original article in Science Digest, July 1980
attestation_log.verification_notes: no fuzzy chunk of quote found in page

attestation_log.source_title: "The Wrong Stuff" — Wired Magazine, Vol. 2 No. 9
attestation_log.author: Rogier van Bakel
attestation_log.lexical_form_seen: moon landing hoax / faked moon landing
attestation_log.exact_quote: "The Wrong Stuff" — Wired profile of Bill Kaysing and the moon landing hoax, September 1994
attestation_log.evidence: Cited in Wikipedia's bibliography for the Moon landing conspiracy theories article. Wired's September 1994 profile of Kaysing brought the 'moon landing hoax' framing to the early internet-era tech-savvy audience. Wired was one of the first major publications to cover this framing for a digitally connected readership.
attestation_log.role_evidence: Wired's 1994 profile introduced the moon landing hoax framing to the early internet-era audience, bridging the pre-web and web eras of the conspiracy's spread.
attestation_log.cited_via: Cited in Wikipedia Moon landing conspiracy theories bibliography as: van Bakel, Rogier (September 1994). "The Wrong Stuff". Wired. Vol. 2, no. 9.

attestation_log.source_title: Conspiracy Theory: Did We Land on the Moon? — Fox Television documentary
attestation_log.author: Fox Broadcasting Company
attestation_log.lexical_form_seen: Did We Land on the Moon? / NASA faked the moon landing
attestation_log.exact_quote: As late as 2001, the Fox television network documentary Conspiracy Theory: Did We Land on the Moon? claimed NASA faked the first landing in 1969 to win the Space Race.
attestation_log.evidence: Broadcast February 15, 2001 on Fox. Confirmed by Wikipedia, Space.com, PolitiFact, and Manchester University. NASA issued a rebuttal fact sheet the day before (Feb 14, 2001). Multiple sources describe this as the single event that most dramatically reinvigorated the 'moon landing hoax' framing in the internet era.
attestation_log.role_evidence: Universally credited as the event that drove the broadest modern public adoption of the 'moon landing hoax' framing, generating massive online discussion in the early internet era.

attestation_log.author: Tony Phillips
attestation_log.evidence: Published February 23, 2001, eight days after the Fox documentary aired. NASA's own Science@NASA web portal used the phrase 'The Great Moon Hoax' in the title of its official rebuttal article, confirming the phrase was already the dominant lexical form in public discourse by this date. Archived and cited in Wikipedia.
attestation_log.role_evidence: NASA's official Science@NASA rebuttal explicitly names and examines the 'moon hoax' framing, functioning as an institutional critic/debunker rather than an adopter.
attestation_log.cited_via: Wikipedia Moon landing conspiracy theories bibliography: Phillips, Tony (February 23, 2001). "The Great Moon Hoax". Science@NASA.

attestation_log.source_title: Bad Astronomy: Misconceptions and Misuses Revealed, from Astrology to the Moon Landing 'Hoax' — book by Phil Plait (Wiley, 2002)
attestation_log.author: Phil Plait
attestation_log.exact_quote: his 2002 book "Bad Astronomy: Misconceptions and Misuses Revealed, from Astrology to the Moon Landing 'Hoax'" (Wiley)
attestation_log.evidence: Published by Wiley in 2002. The book's subtitle contains the diagnostic n-gram 'Moon Landing Hoax' (in scare quotes). Documented by Space.com. Plait's earlier blog post responding to the Fox documentary (February 2001) also used the framing and 'quickly generated thousands of views' per Space.com, making it one of the earliest high-traffic online uses.
attestation_log.role_evidence: Plait's book and blog post explicitly examine and rebut the 'moon landing hoax' framing; the book is a sustained critical/debunking work, not an adoption of the claim.

attestation_log.source_title: "NASA faked the moon landing—therefore, (climate) science is a hoax: An anatomy of the motivated rejection of science" — Psychological Science
attestation_log.author: Stephan Lewandowsky, Klaus Oberauer, Gilles E. Gignac
attestation_log.exact_quote: "NASA faked the moon landing—therefore, (climate) science is a hoax: An anatomy of the motivated rejection of science."
attestation_log.evidence: Published in Psychological Science 24.5 (2013): 622–633. The title of this peer-reviewed academic paper uses the exact diagnostic n-gram 'NASA faked the moon landing' as a named, established belief system being studied. Confirms the framing had achieved sufficient cultural saturation by 2013 to be used as a named variable in academic psychology research.
attestation_log.role_evidence: Academic paper studying the framing as a named conspiracy belief; its function is analytical/critical examination of the claim, not adoption or amplification.
attestation_log.cited_via: Space.com bibliography: Lewandowsky, Stephan, Klaus Oberauer, and Gilles E. Gignac. "NASA faked the moon landing—therefore, (climate) science is a hoax." Psychological Science 24.5 (2013): 622–633.

lexical.adversarial_notes:
Conducted four targeted searches across multiple angles to find any pre-July 1, 1969 instance of the 'moon landing was faked/hoax/staged' narrative framing. The searches covered: (1) general origin history of moon landing conspiracy theories; (2) earliest documented uses of 'faked,' 'hoax,' or 'staged' in relation to the moon landing; (3) Bill Kaysing's publication history and pre-1969 beliefs; and (4) pre-1969 Soviet propaganda, newspaper skepticism, or any anticipatory 'will be faked' framing.

Key findings and ruling-outs:

(a) N-GRAMS AND VARIANTS SEARCHED: 'moon landing hoax,' 'faked moon landing,' 'staged moon landing,' 'never went to the moon,' 'Apollo staged,' 'moon landing conspiracy before 1969,' 'moon landing will be faked,' 'moon landing is faked.' No pre-July 1, 1969 documentary instance of any of these was found.

(b) BILL KAYSING — NEAR MISS BUT NOT A PREDECESSOR: Wikipedia's Bill Kaysing article notes that 'even before July 1969, he had a hunch, an intuition... a true conviction' that no one was going to the Moon. However, this was a private, undocumented personal belief — not a published, broadcast, or otherwise documented public articulation of the framing. His book was self-published in 1976. No evidence exists that he committed this framing to any public record before July 1, 1969.

(c) POST-LANDING SKEPTICISM (RULED OUT AS TOO LATE): The Smithsonian Magazine article cites a New York Times science reporter remarking in December 1969 about 'stool-warmers in Chicago bars' claiming the landing was staged, and an Atlanta Constitution story from June 15, 1970 referencing widespread skepticism. These are post-July 20, 1969 and thus outside scope.

(d) SOVIET PROPAGANDA ANGLE: Multiple sources confirm the Soviet Union — the most motivated party to claim a hoax — did not do so. Pravda ran a front-page story acknowledging the Apollo 11 landing on July 22, 1969, and the Great Soviet Encyclopedia (3rd ed., 1970–1979) described it as a genuine historic event. No Soviet or other foreign pre-landing 'it will be faked' propaganda was found.

(e) FICTIONAL/SATIRICAL PRECURSORS: The 1968 film '2001: A Space Odyssey' is frequently cited in conspiracy lore as a technical precursor (showing realistic Moon footage), but it does not contain or imply a 'moon landing is faked' narrative. The 1971 James Bond film 'Diamonds Are Forever' contains a staged moon-landing scene, but that is post-July 1969. The 1978 film 'Capricorn One' is the major fictional amplifier, also well after the proposed date.

(f) LIMITATIONS: Newspaper archives (ProQuest Historical Newspapers, Chronicling America, paywalled archives like the New York Times archive pre-1969) were not directly accessible via these searches. Google Books snippet view for pre-1969 texts was not directly queried due to search-call limits. Usenet did not exist before 1980. No undigitized pamphlets, zines, or underground press materials from 1967–1969 could be checked. These represent genuine gaps, though the scholarly consensus across Wikipedia, Britannica, History.com, Smithsonian, The Conversation, and University of Manchester is unanimous: the framing did not exist in documented public form before the Apollo 11 landing on July 20, 1969, and did not gain traction until the mid-1970s with Kaysing's 1976 book.

CONCLUSION: The proposed earliest date of 1969-07-01 is structurally impossible to predate in a meaningful sense, because the framing 'the moon landing was faked' is logically contingent on a moon landing having occurred or been imminent. The Apollo 11 landing happened on July 20, 1969 — after the proposed date. The framing could not have existed in its canonical form before the event it describes. The proposed date of 1969-07-01 is therefore not a claim about a pre-event attestation but rather a claim about the very earliest post-event skepticism (i.e., skepticism expressed during the Apollo 11 mission window, July 16–24, 1969). No credible evidence was found of any public articulation of this framing before July 1, 1969. The clean negative result is well-supported.
